(Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court considered a writ petition filed by Garg Inox Ltd & Anr. challenging various demand and payment notices issued in respect of liabilities allegedly arising prior to the initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) on 25.07.2017. The petitioners sought quashing of demands relating to income tax, provident fund, customs, GST and local authority dues pertaining to periods preceding the CIRP commencement date. Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process had been initiated against Petitioner No. 1 under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) by an order dated 25.07.2017 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi. Petitioner No. 2 was the Successful Resolution Applicant. The resolution plan submitted by Petitioner No. 2 was approved by the NCLT on 04.12.2018 under Section 31 of the IBC. The petitioners specifically challenged demand notices issued by the Income Tax Department, including a notice dated 29.05.2020 concerning financial year 2009-10 and an assessment order dated 31.03.2016 concerning assessment year 2013-14. The first demand related to Rs.6,83,244/-, comprising demand of Rs.3,38,280/- and interest of Rs.3,44,964/-, with adjustment against TDS refund. The petitioners also referred to other departmental demands arising from periods preceding the CIRP. The Court noted that an earlier order dated 22.07.2021 had captured the central controversy: after approval of the resolution plan by the NCLT, whether demands relating to dues payable for a period preceding commencement of CIRP could subsequently be raised against the successful resolution applicant. The petitioners relied upon the Supreme Court judgment in Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons Private Limited Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited, particularly paragraph 95. The Supreme Court had held that once a resolution plan is duly approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31, claims provided in the resolution plan become binding, while claims not forming part of the resolution plan stand extinguished and cannot subsequently be pursued. Reliance was also placed on the Supreme Court judgment in Essar Steel India Ltd. Committee of Creditors v. Satish Kumar Gupta, where the Court emphasised that a successful resolution applicant cannot be confronted with undecided claims after approval of the resolution plan. The Court observed that all claims should be submitted to and decided by the resolution professional so that the successful resolution applicant knows the liabilities it is taking over and can operate the corporate debtor on a fresh slate. The Delhi High Court further considered its own Division Bench decisions in Ireo Fiverriver Pvt. Ltd. v. Income Tax Department & Anr. and National Sewing Thread Company Limited v. Deputy Commissioner. In the former, the Court had taken note of Essar Steel and Ghanshyam Mishra and held that a successful resolution applicant cannot be saddled with liabilities other than those specified and factored into the resolution plan. In the latter, the Court reiterated that once a resolution plan is approved, the successful resolution applicant takes over the business on a fresh slate. On a combined reading of these authorities, the Court held that once a resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC, any claim which was not part of that resolution plan stands extinguished and cannot be enforced at a later stage. The Court described the rationale as the “Clean Slate Theory”, intended to provide the resolution applicant with a fresh start free from prior liabilities and to prevent further litigation concerning claims which should have been dealt with during the insolvency resolution process. Applying that principle, the Court found that the impugned claims had arisen prior to 25.07.2017, the date on which CIRP commenced. The demand notice dated 30.09.2019 issued by Respondent No. 4 related to the year 2009-10, while the demand notice dated 18.11.2015 issued by Respondent No. 5 related to 2009-10 and May 2010 to January 2015. The Court therefore held that the “Clean Slate Theory” squarely applied. Accordingly, the writ petition was allowed and the impugned demand notices issued by the respondents concerning claims arising prior to approval of the resolution plan were set aside. Shaifali Steels Limited filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the adjustment of its income tax refunds towards earlier income tax demands. The petitioner sought quashing of the adjustment of refunds aggregating to Rs. 26,86,580/- for Assessment Years 2019-20 to 2023-24 as stated in the prayers, as well as the communication dated 22.01.2026. It also sought processing of the refund without adjustment against income tax demands which, according to the petitioner, had been extinguished pursuant to approval of the resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The petitioner company had undergone Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC. The CIRP was initiated under Section 9 of the IBC and admitted by the Adjudicating Authority on 17.12.2019. An Interim Resolution Professional was appointed and claims were invited from creditors. During the CIRP, the Resolution Plan submitted by M/s. Caxchem Chemical Corporation was approved by the Tribunal on 13.12.2021 under Section 30(6) of the IBC. The Resolution Plan provided for waiver and extinguishment of the unassessed and assessed tax liabilities for the period prior to the Tribunal approval date. The petitioner contended that notwithstanding the approval of the Resolution Plan, the respondent adjusted income tax refunds for Assessment Years 2018-19 to 2023-24 against income tax dues. The petitioner challenged such adjustment on the basis that the relevant tax liabilities had already been extinguished under the approved Resolution Plan. The petitioner also pointed out that, while processing the return for Assessment Year 2024-25, the respondent had processed a refund of Rs. 9,34,830/- without adjusting it against the past dues. On behalf of the petitioner, reliance was placed upon Section 31 of the IBC and the decisions of the Supreme Court in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd. Through Authorised Signatory Vs. Satishkumar Gupta & Ors. and Ghanshyam Mishra and Sons Pvt. Ltd. Through the Authorized Signatory Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. through the Directors & Ors. The petitioner submitted that, upon approval of the Resolution Plan, all dues of the Corporate Debtor except those specifically provided for in the plan stood extinguished. The respondent Department was not in a position to controvert the legal position concerning extinguishment of tax dues under Section 31 of the IBC. The Court examined the relevant provisions of the Resolution Plan. The plan stated that, upon payment of the proposed plan value to the stakeholders, the outstanding dues of the creditors and stakeholders mentioned therein would stand discharged. It further provided that the plan would be binding on the company, creditors, guarantors, members, workmen, employees, Government and semi-Government bodies, authorities and other stakeholders in accordance with Section 31 of the IBC. The plan also stated that it addressed the interests of all stakeholders, including financial creditors, operational creditors, other creditors, guarantors, members, workmen, employees and government bodies. On examination of the Resolution Plan, the Court found that all tax liabilities, assessed and unassessed under the Income Tax Act, 1961, “shall stand waived and extinguished”. The Court then considered the Supreme Court’s ruling in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd., where the Supreme Court emphasised that a successful resolution applicant must be able to take over and run the business on a fresh slate without being confronted with undecided claims after approval of the resolution plan. The Court also considered Ghanshyam Mishra and Sons Pvt. Ltd. Through the Authorized Signatory Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd., in which the Supreme Court held that once a resolution plan is duly approved under Section 31, claims provided in the resolution plan stand frozen and binding, while claims not forming part of the resolution plan stand extinguished. The Supreme Court further held that statutory dues owed to the Central Government, State Government or local authority, if not part of the resolution plan, stand extinguished and proceedings concerning such dues for the period prior to approval under Section 31 cannot be continued. The petitioner challenged, among other things, additions made under Section 2(22)(e) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 towards deemed dividend. A search and seizure action under Section 132 of the Income-tax Act was conducted on 13.10.2017 at several premises of the Delta Group and at the petitioner’s residence. Notices under Section 153A were subsequently issued for Assessment Years 2012-13 to 2017-18, while notice under Section 143(2) was issued for Assessment Year 2018-19. The petitioner had filed settlement applications twice in 2019 and 2020, which were rejected for failure to satisfy the prescribed criteria. A third application filed on 26.02.2021 was dealt with by the Interim Board for Settlement following abolition of the Settlement Commission. In that application, the petitioner admitted undisclosed income of Rs.44,00,000 towards remuneration earned outside banking channels for Assessment Years 2013-14 to 2018-19. The Principal Commissioner of Income Tax submitted a report under Rule 9 of the Income Tax Settlement Commission (Procedure) Rules, stating that additional income of Rs.10,52,32,443 had not been disclosed for Assessment Years 2012-13 to 2018-19. After considering the petitioner’s objection under Rule 9A, the Interim Board did not consider undisclosed income for Assessment Year 2012-13 because there had been no search operation for that year. It accepted certain amounts offered as unaccounted remuneration and unaccounted sales, including Rs.1.25 crore offered as unaccounted sales, holding that such amounts could not be added again. The dispute principally concerned loans received by the petitioner from companies in which he held substantial shareholdings and voting rights. The petitioner had obtained Rs.1,62,88,442 from Delta Aggregates and Sand Pvt Ltd for the financial year relevant to Assessment Year 2014-15, Rs.1.20 crore from Metro Aggregates and Sand India Pvt Ltd in the same financial year, and Rs.11,54,10,055 from Delta M Sand Pvt Ltd for the financial year relevant to Assessment Year 2018-19. The Interim Board treated Rs.4,86,77,012 as deemed dividend under Section 2(22)(e) for Assessment Years 2014-15 and 2018-19. Before the High Court, the petitioner contended that the Settlement Commission could rely only upon material seized during the search and that the additions under Section 2(22)(e) were therefore without jurisdiction. He further contended that assessments under Section 143(3) for Assessment Years 2013-14 and 2014-15 had already been completed without additions on the relevant issues, and that the loans were obtained for business exigencies. Reliance was also placed on the Supreme Court judgment in Principal Commissioner of Income Tax v. Abhisar Buildwell (P) Ltd., the Delhi High Court judgment in Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Creative Dyeing and Printing (P) Ltd., and the Madras High Court judgment in R Chitra v. Vice Chairman, Income Tax Settlement Commission. The High Court rejected the reliance on Abhisar Buildwell, holding that the Supreme Court decision concerned block assessments under Section 153A and not settlement proceedings before the Settlement Commission or Interim Settlement Board. The Court therefore found that the decision had no applicability to the facts of the present case. The Court considered the statutory scheme of Chapter XIX-A. The Court also considered Sections 245E, 245F, 245H, 245I and 245L. On maintainability, the Revenue relied upon the finality contemplated by Section 245-I. The High Court rejected the contention that Section 245-I completely barred judicial review. GST Act, 2017 and IGST Act, 2017 for Financial Years 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 (January). The batch comprised writ petitions filed by M/s Shakti Industries, M/s Rv Pumps, M/s Ishan Industries and Vijay Agarwal. The petitioners submitted that they had been disabled from filing their reply on the Common Portal and, therefore, communications between the parties had taken place through e-mail. In that context, the petitioner asserted that a detailed reply to the Show Cause Notice dated 24.09.2025, together with supporting documents, had been sent on 06.03.2026 to the e-mail address provided by the Adjudicating Authority. However, while passing the impugned order dated 25.03.2026, the Adjudicating Authority recorded that no written submissions/reply had been filed by the petitioner firm and the other three firms even till 09.03.2026. The High Court noted that a specific response had earlier been sought from Revenue to paragraph 18 of the writ petition containing the above assertion. When queried, learned counsel for Revenue stated that he had not received any clear-cut denial of the facts stated in paragraph 18. In these circumstances, the Court considered that no useful purpose would be served by keeping the writ petitions pending or calling for a counter affidavit at that stage. The High Court held that once the reply may have been filed by the petitioner and sent to the Adjudicating Authority on the e-mail provided by that authority, the Adjudicating Authority remained obligated to consider it. The Court held that non-consideration of such reply clearly established violation of the principle of natural justice. Treating this as a fundamental procedural defect in the adjudication proceedings, the Court set aside the impugned order dated 25.03.2026 only in respect of the petitioners involved in the batch. The Adjudicating Authority was directed to fix a fresh date in the proceedings with at least 15 days’ advance notice. The petitioners undertook to cooperate and not seek any undue or long adjournment. After hearing the petitioners, the Adjudicating Authority was permitted to pass a final order, only with respect to the present set of petitioners, as expeditiously as possible and preferably within three months. The prosecution arose from allegations concerning delayed/non-deposit of GST/TDS deducted from payments relating to Gram Sabha development works during the period when the applicants were Gram Pradhan and Gram Panchayat Secretary. The allegation emerging from the enquiry report and FIR, according to the applicants, was confined to Rs.8,629/- of GST/TDS deducted on material purchased for certain Gram Sabha works not being deposited in the Government account within time. The applicants submitted that the entire amount was subsequently deposited upon gaining knowledge of the default and receipts were furnished to the competent authority. They argued that there was no allegation of embezzlement, criminal misappropriation or wrongful gain and that the U.P. Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 constituted a complete and self-contained special statute governing tax deduction, adjudication, penalty and prosecution. The applicants relied upon Sections 51, 122, 126 and 127 of the GST Act and further contended that the alleged occurrence pertained to financial year 2017-18, whereas the FIR dated 19.10.2024, charge sheet dated 01.09.2025 and cognizance order dated 02.04.2026 proceeded under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which came into force subsequently. Reliance was placed upon Sharat Babu Digumarti Vs. Government of NCT of Delhi, 2017 (2) SCC 18, and Deepu & Others Vs. State of U.P., 2024 (8) ILRA 903. The applicants also sought parity with co-accused Tanveer Asharaf Vs. State of U.P. and another, whose proceedings had already been quashed with liberty to the authorities to proceed under the U.P.GST Act, 2017. The High Court examined Sections 50, 51, 122, 125, 126 and 138 of the U.P. Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and held that the GST Act is a complete and self-contained special statute regulating levy, deduction, collection, deposit, adjudication, penalty and prosecution concerning GST liabilities. The Court observed that Section 51 specifically governs tax deduction at source and deposit of the deducted amount, Section 50 provides for interest on delayed payment, Section 122(1)(v) specifically prescribes penalty for failure to deduct or deposit tax under Section 51, Section 125 provides a general penalty, Section 126 contains disciplines relating to penalties, and Section 138 provides for compounding of offences. The Court held that once the field is specifically occupied by a special statute providing an exhaustive mechanism, resort to general penal law could be justified only where the allegations independently disclose ingredients of distinct criminal offences such as dishonest misappropriation, forgery, fabrication of records, cheating or wrongful gain. On examining the FIR and charge sheet, the Court found no allegation of embezzlement of Government funds, dishonest misappropriation, siphoning for personal use, fabrication or manipulation of records, fake transactions, forged documents, dishonest withdrawal or wrongful gain. The amount allegedly not deposited had also subsequently been deposited. Accordingly, the allegations fell within the statutory framework of the U.P. GST Act and not within Section 316(5) BNS. On the second issue, the Court noted that the alleged omission related to financial year 2017-18, whereas the FIR, charge sheet and cognizance proceedings invoked the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Following Deepu (supra), the Court held that while investigation after commencement of the new criminal laws may proceed according to the procedure prescribed under BNSS, the substantive offence cannot be altered by a subsequently enforced penal statute. Since Section 316(5) BNS was not in existence on the date of the alleged occurrence, the prosecution under that provision suffered from manifest legal infirmity. The High Court therefore held that continuation of the criminal proceedings would amount to abuse of process and quashed the charge sheet, cognizance/summoning order and proceedings against the applicants. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vattikundala Prabhakara Rao Vs ITO (ITAT Chennai) Summary: ITAT Chennai allowed the appeal of a retired ONGC employee and held that he was eligible for the enhanced exemption limit of Rs.25,00,000 under Section 10(10AA)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of leave encashment received on retirement for AY 2020-21. The assessee retired from ONGC on 31.05.2019 and received Rs.40,23,450 towards leave encashment as a superannuation benefit. For TDS purposes, exemption had been considered only up to Rs.3 lakh. While filing his return on 14.09.2020 declaring income of Rs.26,42,386, the assessee claimed enhanced exemption relying upon the Delhi High Court decision in Kamal Kumar Kalia & Ors. Vs Union of India & Ors.. The return was processed under Section 143(1), restricting the exemption and determining total income at Rs.63,65,840. CIT(A) dismissed the appeal on the basis that the applicable notified ceiling for a non-Government employee was Rs.3 lakh. The appeal before the Tribunal was delayed by 1,023 days. The assessee explained that he had been waiting for a judicial development after the CIT(A)’s order and filed the appeal after learning of subsequent Tribunal rulings concerning CBDT Notification No.31/2023 dated 24.05.2023. ITAT followed its Coordinate Bench decision in Balasubramanian Venkatachalaperumal Vs DCIT, where an analogous delay of 1,165 days had been condoned. Relying upon Collector, Land Acquisition Vs. MST.Katiji & Ors., the Tribunal found reasonable and sufficient cause and condoned the delay. On merits, the Tribunal again followed Balasubramanian Venkatachalaperumal, which had examined whether the enhanced Rs.25 lakh ceiling introduced through CBDT Notification No.31/2023 could benefit a non-Government employee for AY 2020-21. That decision regarded the enhancement as beneficial and remedial, intended to rationalise the long-standing Rs.3 lakh ceiling and mitigate hardship. The Coordinate Bench had also relied upon decisions including Ram Dev Daiya Vs ITO, Govardhan Deepchand Bhambhani Vs ITO, Govind Chhatwani Vs CIT (Appeals), Ram Charan Gupta Vs ITO, Devi Dutt Agarwal Vs Assessment Unit, Chandra Prakash Vashistha Vs ITO and Vijay Kumar Jain Vs ITO. Considering that the facts of the assessee’s case were identical to the Coordinate Bench decision, ITAT Chennai held that the assessee was eligible for the enhanced exemption limit of Rs.25,00,000 under Section 10(10AA)(ii) in respect of leave encashment received on retirement. The Assessing Officer was directed to allow the exemption in accordance with the directions contained in the Coordinate Bench decision. The assessee’s appeal was accordingly allowed. (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: CESTAT Ahmedabad dismissed four Revenue appeals seeking personal penalties against Shri Kamilbhai Z. Vashi and other co-noticees after noting that Revenue’s appeal against the main assessee, M/s. Taha Wires Pvt Ltd, arising from the same adjudication order had already been dismissed. The dispute originated from a Show Cause Notice dated 03.10.2007 alleging wrongful availment of CENVAT credit of Rs.3,93,98,286/- on copper ingots/wire bars of Sri Lankan origin allegedly without actual receipt of the inputs. Penalties had also been proposed against the director and transporters under Rule 26 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 and other provisions. DGCEI had alleged that Taha Wires used non-duty-paid scrap for manufacturing copper wires while availing CENVAT credit on duty-paid invoices without physically receiving the invoiced inputs. The original adjudication order dated 20.04.2011 confirmed demands, interest and penalties. However, CESTAT, by order dated 08.01.2019, set aside that order and remanded the matter for de novo adjudication. In the remand proceedings, the Principal Commissioner, Central GST & Central Excise, Daman, passed the Order-in-Original dated 16.07.2019 in favour of the noticees by dropping the proceedings. Revenue thereafter filed separate appeals against Taha Wires and the four co-noticees. The Tribunal recorded that Revenue’s appeal against the main respondent, Taha Wires Pvt Ltd, had already been dismissed vide Final Order No. A/10092/2022 dated 11.02.2022. In that order, the Tribunal had found that Revenue failed to establish clandestine diversion of the disputed inputs or substitution thereof by locally procured scrap. There was no evidence identifying alleged buyers, no evidence of transportation or financial flow-back relating to diversion, and no evidence regarding procurement of substituted scrap. On the other hand, statutory records, bank payments, CHA records, job-work challans, job-work registers and RG23A Part-I & II supported actual receipt and utilisation of the inputs. The earlier order also noted that all 124 consignments were supported by job-work records under Rule 4(5)(a) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 read with Notification No. 214/86-CE. No discrepancies were found during searches at the assessee’s factory or the job worker’s premises. The case rested principally on third-party evidence such as transporter statements, RTO records and check-post records, while such statements were either retracted or contradicted in cross-examination. CESTAT had therefore upheld the dropping of proceedings against Taha Wires. In the present appeals, the Departmental Representative admitted that the appeal against the main assessee had been dismissed and further stated that no new grounds had been taken for imposing penalties upon the present respondents. CESTAT held that once the appeal against the principal assessee had been dismissed, nothing survived against the co-noticees in the absence of any independent or new ground for personal penalty. The Tribunal accordingly held that personal penalties could not be imposed, found no merit in Revenue’s appeals and dismissed all four appeals. rows.desc: EconomyRBI Forex Swap Window Attracts $136.37 Billion, FCNR(B) Deposits Drive InflowsCurated by: Vikas KumarUpdated Sep 2, 2026, 19:37 ISTFCNR(B) deposits scheme was originally open till September 30, 2026, was advanced to close on August 31, 2026, due to unexpected inflows.RBI Forex Swap Windowfollow usfollow usThe special USD-INR forex swap facility by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has attracted total inflows of $136.37 billion as of August 31, 2026, according to data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).In the total inflows, FCNR(B) deposits emerged as the dominant contributor, accounting for $127.22 billion of the total inflows. This is nearly 90 per cent of the overall figure. OFCBs added $5.26 billion, while ECBs brought in $3.89 billion.FCNR(B) deposits scheme was originally open till September 30, 2026, was advanced to close on August 31, 2026, due to unexpected inflows.A special USD-INR forex swap facility was introduced by RBI covering these instruments on June 8 this year to deal with forex outflows. This was due to high oil prices and flight of capital owing to exit of Foreign Portfolio Investors (FOIs) from the stock market. The rupee had come under pressure when these measures were announced. The early closure aims to cap dollar inflows that have already outpaced the $26 billion raised in 2013, when then RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan launched a similar swap scheme. Back then, the rupee appreciated by 2.84 per cent against the dollar in over two months. This time, the rupee gained 0.18 per cent around the same number of months. The RBI’s special swap measures mobilised a higher-than-expected $136.4 billion in foreign currency inflows till August 31. The rupee on Thursday settled at 94.49 per dollar, its strongest close since June 25. The rupee had closed at 94.98 on Wednesday. During the session, it touched an intraday high of 94.27 per dollar. The rupee has gained more than 1 per cent in the last week, making it one of Asia’s best-performing currencies. Market participants said dollar inflows have strengthened the RBI’s hand in managing pressure on the rupee at a time when elevated crude oil prices and rising global bond yields have weighed on emerging-market currencies. In the early stages of the FCNR(B) scheme, the rupee’s appreciation remained muted due to a stronger influence of global factors on the local currency. However, dealers said the RBI has since stepped up direct intervention in the spot market to contain volatility in the exchange rate. } } Home / Finance / News / Revolving credit ban will impact a larger section, NBFCs tell RBIRevolving credit ban will impact a larger section, NBFCs tell RBIIndustry seeks clarity on products allowing limited redraw and supply-chain finance, as well as whether recovery calls can be made through the mandated 1600-number series premium | Image: BloombergAnupreksha Jain Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Sep 03 2026 | 10:25 PM IST @media (min-width:1100px) and (max-width:1280px) { .storymeta .meta-info { flex: 0 0 45%; } } Listen to This ArticleThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) recent proposal to ban revolving credit offered by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) would impact a larger section of players and products, as compared to what was estimated earlier, the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) told the regulator on Thursday. FIDC is a self-regulatory organisation for shadow banks. The FIDC and representatives of NBFCs met RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu and shared their feedback. The Council urged the regulator to rethink the decision on such a blanket ban, sources told Business Standard. “Initially, the impact was seen to be limited to three or four NBFCs. But the feedback has shown that a much larger section of the industry could be impacted. The RBI may, therefore, look at a partial restriction rather than a blanket ban,” an NBFC chief executive said. Around 30-40 lenders have submitted their responses to FIDC. All suggestions discussed by the industry will be consolidated and sent to the RBI through the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), sources said. “The RBI is still receiving a lot of views. The purpose of putting out a draft is to take the public view, absorb the feedback, and then convert it into regulation,” another NBFC chief executive said. A key concern for lenders is the treatment of products that allow limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility. NBFCs have argued that such facilities do not necessarily constitute the kind of revolving lending that the RBI seeks to restrict. “The issue is that there is something in between a conventional term loan and what the RBI may be defining as revolving credit. There are products that technically may not fit neatly into the definition, and that is where the industry has sought greater clarity,” an industry executive said. Supply chain finance is another area where NBFCs have sought an exemption or specific clarification. Lenders said such financing is closely monitored through goods and services tax (GST) data, and that loans are disbursed directly to suppliers rather than borrowers. The RBI's proposal is aimed at ensuring repayment discipline and addressing concerns around borrower creditworthiness and loan evergreening. NBFCs, however, have said a broad definition could capture legitimate lending products. “The industry is not opposed to the objective of preventing evergreening or ensuring borrower credibility. The concern is over a blanket definition that could capture products which are not being used for that purpose,” an another NBFC chief executive said. The final guidelines on revolving credit could take another two months as the RBI assesses the feedback before deciding on the scope of restrictions. Separately, NBFCs have sought clarity on whether recovery calls can be made through the 1600-number series mandated for service and transactional calls by regulated financial entities. “Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source said. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) has mandated regulated financial entities to use the 1600 series for service and transactional voice calls. NBFCs said the framework could create difficulties

The moderation in revolving credit is partly structural, as consumers have become more conscious of making timely repayments, while digital platforms and payment reminders have reduced instances of customers inadvertently carrying balances, the bank said. Speaking after the launch of the Axis Bank-Scapia co-branded credit card, Dixit said, “Revolvers have been coming down for roughly five years.” She said the trend was a combination of industry evolution and the credit cycle, with greater consumer awareness and multiple platforms and mechanisms reminding customers to pay their dues on time, reducing instances of accidental revolving. The moderation in revolvers, however, does not necessarily mean weaker growth in the overall credit card book. Point-of-sale transactions converted into equated monthly instalments (EMIs) can continue to generate revenue-accretive spending and support growth in card receivables. “Newly acquired customers also take time to contribute meaningfully to the book. rows.title: RBI DG Murmu meets FIDC, NBFC CEOs; may rethink blanket ban on revolving credit
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read RBI DG Murmu meets FIDC, NBFC CEOs; may rethink blanket ban on revolving credit RBI may reconsider its proposed blanket ban on revolving credit facilities by non bank lenders after receiving feedback that the draft could affect a much wider section of the NBFC industry than initially envisaged, sources told ETBFSI. RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu recently held a meeting with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC), having already received 350 feedbacks from the industry. Exemption to Supply chain financing has garnered repeated attention, with one of the senior industry participant saying final guidelines may come in another two months. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 06:53 PM IST var news_msid = 133737739; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The Reserve Bank of India may reconsider its proposed blanket ban on revolving credit facilities by non bank lenders after receiving feedback that the draft could affect a much wider section of the NBFC industry than initially envisaged, sources said.RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu recently held a meeting with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to discuss the proposed restrictions on revolving credit, with the central bank listening to concerns raised by lenders, according to people aware of the discussions.The RBI had initially envisaged the impact of the proposed ban to be limited to around three to four NBFCs. However, feedback received during the consultation has indicated that a significantly larger section of the industry could be affected, prompting the central bank to consider whether a blanket prohibition is appropriate, sources said. Advt “Initially, the impact was seen as being limited to three or four NBFCs. But the feedback has shown that a much larger section of the industry could be impacted. RBI may therefore look at a partial restriction rather than a blanket ban,” an NBFC CEO said.The contours of any changes are yet to be finalised, the person added and all the suggestions discussed will be sent to RBI by Confederation of Indian Industry (CII). The development comes after substantial industry feedback on the draft. Around 30-40 lenders have submitted their responses to FIDC, while the RBI has received around 350 responses on the proposed revolving credit restrictions, according to sources.“RBI is still receiving a lot of views. The purpose of putting out a draft is to take the public view, absorb the feedback and then convert it into regulation,” another NBFC CEO said.The RBI's proposal had raised concerns across the NBFC industry over the scope of its definition of revolving credit and its potential impact on products and lending structures that are not necessarily intended to perpetually roll over credit.The central bank's concern behind the proposal is linked to the credibility and creditworthiness of borrowers, sources said. The proposed framework seeks to ensure greater discipline around the repayment and continuation of credit facilities rather than allowing credit limits to remain available on a revolving basis. Advt However, NBFCs have argued that there are several products where limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility does not necessarily amount to the kind of revolving lending that RBI is seeking to restrict.“The issue is that there is something in between a conventional term loan and what RBI may be defining as revolving credit. There are products that technically may not fit neatly into the definition, and that is where the industry has sought greater clarity,” an industry professional said.The industry has also pointed to the potential impact on working-capital and other lending products if the definition is applied too broadly. Advt “RBI has been quite positive in the discussions and is listening to the points being raised by the industry. That gives us confidence that the feedback will be considered before the final regulation,” an NBFC CEO said.The issue is not new, with NBFCs having raised concerns around the treatment of revolving credit with the RBI in earlier discussions as well. However, the latest draft has brought the issue into sharper focus by putting the proposed restrictions in writing.“There were discussions on the same issue even earlier, but there were no guidelines in writing. The moment something is put into a regulation, the grey areas become much more important because businesses have to comply with the exact wording,” an industry professional said. Advt The consultation process is therefore expected to play a key role in determining whether RBI retains the blanket restriction or introduces exemptions or a more targeted prohibition.Sources said the final guidelines could take another two months to be issued, giving the central bank time to assess the responses received from lend

rows.title: NBFCs nudge RBI on TRAI’s 1600 series rules for recovery calls
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read NBFCs nudge RBI on TRAI’s 1600 series rules for recovery calls Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 07:06 PM IST var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.RBI regulated entities covered by the mandate are not permitted to initiate service or transactional voice calls from numbers other than those allocated under the 1600 series, even where they have explicit or inferred customer consent.TRAI's stated objective is to prevent promotional calls from being made under the guise of service or transactional calls and to give BFSI entities a distinct identity that allows consumers to make informed decisions about whether to answer a call.However, NBFCs said the framework does not clearly address recovery communications. Lenders typically make large volumes of calls to borrowers regarding overdue payments, repayment schedules and other recovery-related matters, and the industry wants to know whether such calls qualify as service calls under the 1600 framework.“The distinction between a sales call, a service call and a recovery call is important. I agree that a sales call should not be made through 1600. But whether a recovery call is considered a service call is not clear,” the NBFC CEO said.The concern is compounded by the possibility of customers blocking calls originating from the 1600 series. Industry participants said that while the dedicated series is intended to help consumers identify genuine financial-sector calls, borrowers may still block such numbers as unwanted or spam, particularly when they receive repeated recovery calls. Advt “If you are doing mass recovery calls and people are blocking those numbers, the whole purpose is lost,” the source said.According to the industry, the problem becomes particularly acute when a borrower does not respond to repeated calls from a lender’s 1600 number.“Imagine a 1600 call. If the customer does not pick up, how will a banker communicate? If we try once or twice and the number is blocked, can we then call from our normal number? That is the question,” the CEO said. rows.title: RBI DG Murmu says NBFCs should use securitisation to transfer risk, free up capital
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read RBI DG Murmu says NBFCs should use securitisation to transfer risk, free up capital RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu has called for securitisation to evolve beyond a liquidity management tool into a mechanism for genuine risk transfer and capital release, while urging NBFCs and HFCs to diversify funding sources amid vulnerabilities exposed by past liquidity shocks. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 3, 2026 at 12:58 PM IST var news_msid = 133729017; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Reserve Bank of India (RBI) deputy governor Shirish Chandra MurmuThe Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu has called for securitisation to move beyond being a liquidity management tool and become a genuine mechanism for transferring risk and freeing up capital, as the non-banking financial sector enters a new phase of growth.Speaking at the 7th edition of the NBFC and HFC Summit in Mumbai, Murmu said the growing role of non bank lenders in India's credit system also brings the need for stronger foundations, particularly around liquidity management, asset quality and governance. Advt “Securitisation should also grow beyond liquidity tools into a genuine way to transfer risk and free up capital,” Murmu said, adding that this should be accompanied by appropriate scaling and transparency rules.The RBI deputy governor also flagged funding concentration as a key vulnerability for NBFCs and HFCs. Past liquidity events, he said, have demonstrated how exposed non-bank lenders can be to shifts in market sentiment and concentration in funding sources.“Strong liquidity risk management is not optional,” Murmu said, calling on entities to diversify their funding sources. He also said a deep and liquid corporate bond market would help the sector in this regard, with RBI continuing to work with market participants to develop such a market.Murmu's comments come against the backdrop of the expanding role of NBFCs in India's credit ecosystem. Credit extended by NBFCs is now above 16.7 per cent of nominal GDP, compared with 15.9 per cent a year earlier, while it accounts for about 27 per cent of the credit extended by scheduled commercial banks, up from 26 per cent a year earlier.According to Murmu, the sector is increasingly moving from being a set of alternative lenders to becoming a group of specialised financial partners that complement banks. NBFCs and HFCs have built expertise in areas including supply-chain finance, infrastructure debt, affordable housing, vehicle finance and gold and silver-backed lending. Advt This specialisation, he said, allows lenders to assess borrowers using more than traditional metrics and structure credit around their cash flows. Co-lending arrangements with banks can further extend the reach of such specialised lenders.“Growth must never come at the cost of underwriting standards,” he said.The RBI deputy governor also outlined the regulatory changes introduced over the past five to six years to strengthen the foundations of the non-banking sector. These include the comprehensive liquidity risk management framework introduced in 2019, phased capital requirements from 2020 and the scale-based regulatory framework introduced in 2021, which calibrates regulation according to an NBFC's size, activities and risk. Advt RBI subsequently consolidated the framework and introduced measures covering fraud risk management, internal audit, supervisory reporting and compliance requirements. At the same time, the central bank has taken steps intended to support sustainable growth, including regulatory flexibility for certain activities and exemptions for some smaller NBFCs from registration requirements.Murmu said RBI's approach to digital finance has also been to avoid creating a separate regulatory framework. Instead, the central bank follows the principle of “substance over form”, adapting existing rules to new digital contexts while maintaining proportionate regulation and financial stability. Advt Five priorities for NBFCsMurmu identified five priorities for sustainable growth of the sector - governance and culture, liquidity management, asset quality and credit risk, customer protection and fair conduct, and digital transformation and cyber resilience. rows.title: After record FCNR inflows, will domestic deposit rates finally fall?
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read After record FCNR inflows, will domestic deposit rates finally fall? The funding windfall could ease pressure on banks to compete aggressively for domestic deposits, particularly bulk deposits, as the FCNR(B) deposits carry regulatory advantages. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Updated On Sep 3, 2026 at 05:24 AM IST var news_msid = 133722508; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Banks mobilised $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits by August 31, taking total inflows under the swap facility to $136.38 billion.Fresh domestic term-deposit rates fell to 5.90% in July from 5.99% in June, while outstanding deposit rates remained at 6.58%.SBI cut bulk deposit rates by up to 25 basis points across several short-tenor buckets, signalling easing pressure on domestic funding costs.FCNR inflows could support bank margins by reducing reliance on expensive domestic funding, but a broad-based fall in deposit rates will depend on credit demand and deposit mobilisation.India’s record mobilisation of foreign-currency deposits is creating room for banks to reduce their dependence on expensive domestic funding, raising the prospect of further declines in deposit rates. The latest data show fresh domestic term-deposit rates have already started easing, while the scale of FCNR(B) mobilisation has significantly strengthened banks’ funding position.Banks mobilised $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits under the Reserve Bank of India’s special foreign-exchange swap facility by August 31, taking total inflows under the facility to $136.38 billion, including $5.26 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings and $3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings. The FCNR(B) mobilisation window closed on August 31, while the ECB and OFCB windows remain open until December 31. Advt The funding windfall could ease pressure on banks to compete aggressively for domestic deposits, particularly bulk deposits, as the FCNR(B) deposits carry regulatory advantages. Eligible three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits mobilised under the scheme are exempt from CRR and SLR requirements, reducing the regulatory cost associated with these funds.There are already signs of moderation in domestic deposit pricing. The weighted average domestic term-deposit rate on fresh deposits declined to 5.90% in July from 5.99% in June, while the rate on outstanding deposits remained unchanged at 6.58%. The decline, however, predates the final surge in FCNR(B) mobilisation and therefore cannot be attributed solely to the foreign-currency inflows.The pressure on domestic funding costs is also visible in banks’ pricing of bulk deposits. State Bank of India cut rates on deposits of Rs 3 crore and above by 25 basis points across several short-tenor buckets from August 15, while rates on some other tenors were reduced by 10 basis points.Varied impactThe impact of the FCNR mobilisation is likely to differ across banks. Larger banks with stronger access to foreign-currency deposits may have greater scope to replace relatively expensive domestic bulk funding, whereas smaller banks could remain more dependent on domestic deposits to support credit growth. Advt The funding advantage comes at a time when the transmission of lower policy rates to bank lending rates remains uneven. Outstanding WALR on rupee loans rose marginally to 8.97% in July from 8.96% in June, while WALR on fresh loans declined marginally to 8.52% from 8.53%. The one-year median MCLR, meanwhile, increased to 8.70% in August from 8.60% in July.This divergence could become important for bank margins. If deposit costs decline faster than lending rates, banks could see some relief on their funding costs even as loan pricing remains relatively sticky. However, the benefit will not flow through immediately because a large part of banks’ existing deposit book is repriced only when deposits mature and are renewed. Advt With the FCNR(B) mobilisation window now closed, the key question is how much of the funding benefit translates into lower domestic deposit rates. The initial signs point towards easing pressure on deposit pricing, but a broad-based decline will depend on banks’ credit demand, the pace of domestic deposit mobilisation and how quickly the additional foreign-currency funding is deployed.For now, the record FCNR(B) inflow has changed the funding equation for banks, but it is too early to conclude that it will by itself trigger a sustained fall in domestic deposit rates. rows.title: Niva Bupa hikes premiums 8-9% annually to keep pace with medical inflation: CFO Vishwanath Mahendra
rows.desc: Articles 7 min read Niva Bupa hikes premiums 8-9% annually to keep pace with medical inflation: CFO Vishwanath Mahendra Niva Bupa Health Insurance is prioritising profitable growth even as medical inflation continues to push up the cost of health cover, with the insurer raising premiums by around 8-9% annually and expecting this trend to continue. CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said smaller annual increases are preferable to sharp hikes every few years, while the insurer targets a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE. Anushka Sengupta ETBFSI Published On Aug 29, 2026 at 08:08 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133602500; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Vishwanath Mahendra, CFO, Niva Bupa Health InsuranceNiva Bupa Health Insurance is seeing strong growth, with retail health premium rising 47% year-on-year in Q1, significantly ahead of the industry’s 32% growth. Overall premium grew 32%, while profit after tax nearly doubled 93% to Rs 138 crore, even as the insurer remained selective in group health amid an unfavourable pricing environment.But the growth is coming against a persistent challenge for the health insurance industry: rising medical inflation and the resulting pressure on premiums. Niva Bupa CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said the insurer has already raised premiums by 8-9% annually, and expects this to continue as medical costs rise, arguing that smaller, regular hikes are preferable to a sharp increase every few years. Advt Mahendra also said Niva Bupa is targeting profitable growth, with a medium-term goal of a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE, while its retail market share has crossed 11%.Here are the edited excerpts from the interview:Q. By how much has Niva Bupa raised its premiums this year to tackle rising medical inflation. Should customers expect another round of hikes next year as well?Vishwanath: Medical inflation is something which is eating every day now. Ultimately, we have to pass on that to policyholders because there is no other way if we want to make the product sustainable in the long run.We have been increasing premiums in high single digits in the past, and we would like to continue doing that. Rather than increasing premiums once in three years by a big number, our preference is to increase them by only single digits every year, so that it is not as much of a pinch for policyholders.So, when I say 8-9%, I mean 8-9% per annum, which will be experienced by policyholders. And yes, this is something we expect to continue next year as well.Of course, we are also doing many other things, discussions with hospitals on treatment protocols, industry initiatives and care pathways, to ensure there are no unnecessary admissions, abuse or wastage. But at some point, inflation is there in the economy and we have to pass that on. Advt Q. Your retail health business grew 47% in Q1, much faster than the industry. Is that growth coming at healthy economics or are you sacrificing margins to gain market share?Vishwanath: It is coming from healthy economics. The growth is being driven by investment across distribution channels, product innovation and our claims practices.We have been investing across agency, bancassurance, direct-to-consumer and third-party channels. Our newly launched product, ReAssure 3.0, has also been received very well by distributors and customers.Our claim settlement ratio is close to 96%, and we are not compromising on underwriting or profitability to drive growth. Advt Q. You have also kept group health growth largely flat. Was that a conscious decision because pricing was not attractive?Vishwanath: Yes. We generally write business only if it is value-accretive. The pricing environment in group health was not very supportive, so we decided to stay away from business that was not economically attractive.We continue to focus on segments within group health which are good businesses from a profitability perspective. The approach is very clear, we want profitable growth, not growth at any cost.Q. With 32% overall growth and 93% growth in profit after tax, how close are you to consistently generating underwriting profits? Advt Vishwanath: We are very much there. It is only a matter of 20 basis points. Our combined insurance service ratio has improved by 300 basis points, from 103.2% to 100.2%.Our medium-term guidance since listing has been mid-to-high teens ROE, which corresponds to a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29. We are very much on that trajectory.Our post-tax ROE was 11.8% for the last four rolling quarters, so the trajectory is very much there.Q. Retail market share has crossed 11%. How much further do you want to take it?Vishwanath: Our target is to keep growing retail health at least 8-10% higher than the industry and keep gaining market share ever

rows.title: September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising Jio's proposed Rs 37,700-crore issue has already received Sebi approval, while NSE's proposed Rs 30,000-crore issue could significantly add to September's fundraising if launched. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 1, 2026 at 01:02 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133672651; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook JIO, NSE ఐపీఓలు.. ఇండియా స్టాక్ మార్కెట్ చరిత్ర తిరగరాయడం ఖాయమా?September’s IPO calendar has opened with mainboard issues from Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief, alongside SME offerings.More than 25 companies are expected to tap the IPO market, with Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health among the larger names in the broader pipeline.Improved market sentiment and stronger listing gains have revived IPO activity after a subdued first half of CY26.Despite strong average IPO returns, wide variations in post-listing performance underline the need for selective stock picking.September could emerge as one of the biggest months for India’s primary market, with more than 25 companies expected to tap the IPO market and potential mega issues from Jio Platforms and the National Stock Exchange (NSE) capable of pushing monthly fundraising towards Rs 70,000 crore.The month has opened with a busy primary-market calendar. Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief are among the mainboard offerings around the start of September, while Farm Peace, Phychem Technologies, Shanti Inorganics and Ashutosh Fibre are among the SME issues. The seven issues identified in the opening-week calendar together are looking to raise more than Rs 1,400 crore. Advt The biggest potential trigger, however, is Jio Platforms. The company has received Sebi approval for a proposed IPO of around Rs 37,700 crore, which would make it India's largest IPO if launched at that size. NSE is also considering a public issue of around Rs 30,000 crore, although its launch timing has not been confirmed.If either of the two mega issues comes to market in September, fundraising could rise sharply, with the month's total potentially approaching Rs 70,000 crore depending on the issue launched, its final size and the broader IPO pipeline.The possibility of a record September comes after a sharp revival in primary-market activity in July and August. Companies raised more than Rs 28,000 crore through IPOs in July, while 22 companies raised over Rs 23,000 crore in August. The August fundraising was the highest in a year in terms of the number of companies accessing the market.The revival follows a subdued first half of CY26, when market volatility, valuation concerns, foreign investor outflows and geopolitical tensions weighed on IPO activity. The Nifty 50 fell around 9% during H1 CY26, prompting several companies to defer their fundraising plans.Primary market boomMarket conditions improved in July and August, helping restore investor appetite. The Nifty 50 gained around 1.8% from the end of June through the first two months of the second half, while IPO listing performance improved substantially.The average listing-day gain of 25 IPOs that debuted between July 1 and August 19 stood at 20.9%, compared with 1.72% in H1 CY26. Across 47 mainboard IPOs during the year, the average listing gain was 11.9%. Advt The stronger listing performance has provided a more favourable backdrop for September's IPO pipeline. Companies that had held back their plans amid weaker market conditions now have greater incentive to proceed, while merchant bankers have a sizeable pool of approved and filed offerings to bring to market.The broader pipeline includes large companies such as Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health, among others. However, these companies should not be treated as confirmed September IPOs, as their launch dates have not been announced.The pipeline remains sizeable. Since March 2025, 146 companies have received Sebi approval, while 67 are awaiting regulatory approval, 65 have filed DRHPs and another 33 have filed confidential DRHPs. This gives the primary market a substantial pool of potential issuers beyond the current September calendar. Advt The surge in IPO activity will nevertheless test the market's ability to absorb a large supply of new equity. Large offerings from Jio Platforms and potentially NSE could compete for institutional and retail liquidity with smaller mainboard and SME issues coming to market at the same time.Investor returns also remain uneven despite the improvement in sentiment. The average gain from issue price across 407 IPOs stood at 66% as of July 31, but 17% of companies were trading 25-50% below their issue price and another 9% were more than 50% below the issue price. rows.title: HDFC Bank, Kotak, Axis seen as re-rating candidates despite Q1 margin pressure
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read HDFC Bank, Kotak, Axis seen as re-rating candidates despite Q1 margin pressure NII growth for the banking sector rose to a multi-quarter high of 11% YoY in Q1FY27, while core PPOP and PAT growth improved to 15-17% YoY, supported by contained operating expenses and stable provisioning. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Aug 24, 2026 at 07:00 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133445973; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook AI-generated image for representationLarge private banks lagged peers, with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank reporting around 1% QoQ NII growth and 7-9% YoY growth as NIMs declined.FCNR(B) inflows of US$52 billion could support bank NII and EPS, with lower landed funding costs potentially aiding domestic NIMs.Asset quality remained supportive, with overall gross slippages at 1.2% versus 1.4% a year earlier; Axis and Kotak reported among thelowest quarterly slippages after adjusting for seasonality.HDFC Bank, Kotak and Axis valuations are seen as compelling, while rising NII growth and leadership clarity at HDFC Bank and Kotak could provide re-rating catalystsLarge private banks could be re-rating candidates in FY27 despite weak Q1FY27 margin performance, as rising sector-wide NII growth, benign asset quality and liquidity, and potential clarity on MD&CEO reappointment or succession could provide catalysts for HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, while improving NII growth could support the broader large-private-bank segment.NII growth for the banking sector rose to a multi-quarter high of 11% YoY in Q1FY27, while core PPOP and PAT growth improved to 15-17% YoY, supported by contained operating expenses and stable provisioning. Large private banks, however, lagged peers, with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank each reporting around 1% QoQ NII growth and 7-9% YoY growth as NIMs declined by double digits sequentially. Current valuations for the three large private banks are seen as compelling, while clarity on MD&CEO reappointment or succession at HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, along with rising NII growth, could act as re-rating catalysts, ICICI Securities said. Advt The margin weakness comes even as private banks accelerated loan growth. Private banks grew loans around 4% QoQ in Q1FY27, ahead of 2% for PSBs, led by acceleration at HDFC Bank and Axis Bank. Systemic loan growth reached around 18% YoY in Q1FY27, while systemic credit growth is estimated at around 15% for FY27, with broadly similar growth expected from PSBs and private banks.The pressure on large private bank margins was linked partly to changes in loan and funding mix. Yield on advances softened for banks with a higher contribution from wholesale growth, while the cost of funds turned adverse for most banks due to elevated bulk deposit rates, adverse CASA movement and receding term-deposit repricing.The outlook for NII growth could improve as FCNR(B) mobilisation strengthens. FCNR(B) inflows reached US$52 billion, or around 2% of outstanding deposits, as of August 13, while the RBI has curtailed the mobilisation window to the end of August from the earlier end-September deadline. The deposits are expected to be growth, NII and EPS accretive, with lower landed funding costs potentially supporting domestic NIMs.NIM trajectoryThe impact on overall NIMs, however, will depend on the growth of overseas books, competition and movements in spreads. NII growth therefore remains an important earnings indicator alongside NIM, particularly while asset quality and liquidity remain favourable. Advt Asset quality provides additional support to the sector's earnings outlook. Overall gross slippages were 1.2% in Q1FY27, lower than 1.4% a year earlier. Private bank slippages improved YoY, although they remained elevated at around 1.7% compared with around 0.7% for PSBs. Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank recorded among the lowest quarterly slippages after adjusting for Q1 seasonality.Banks also maintained cost discipline, with core PPOP growth of around 17% YoY outpacing NII growth. Stable credit costs contributed to around 15% YoY growth in PAT across the coverage universe, with private banks reporting 16% growth and PSBs 14%. Advt For large private banks, the key question through FY27 will be whether NII growth can accelerate while margins stabilise and asset quality remains benign. FCNR(B) mobilisation could provide support to funding costs and earnings, while leadership clarity at HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank could provide an additional valuation catalyst.The positive sector view therefore remains intact despite the weak Q1 margin performance at large private banks, with their current valuations seen as compelling and rising NII growth offering scope for a potential re-rating. By ETBFSI Research , ETBFSI Published On Aug 24, 2026 at 07:00 AM IST Telegram Fa

rows.title: Why NCLT approved Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.5-crore proposal despite financial creditor rejection
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read Why NCLT approved Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.5-crore proposal despite financial creditor rejection Why did the NCLT approve the extremely low Rs 6.5-crore plan proposed by Dr Subhash Chandra, which amounts to just 0.03% of the total claims of Rs 22,006 crore? The major reason behind the approval was the voting pattern among creditors. Chandra had also not provided personal guarantees for the entire Rs 22,006 crore, but for a significantly smaller amount. Here are the details based on the 144-page NCLT order. Amol Dethe ETBFSI Updated On Aug 28, 2026 at 08:28 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133581637; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The National Company Law Tribunal's approval of Subhash Chandra's Rs 6.5-crore repayment plan, against Rs 22,006 crore of admitted claims, was driven by the voting outcome among creditors and the tribunal's reliance on their commercial wisdom.While several financial creditors opposed the plan over the low recovery, creditors representing about 80% of the voting share backed it. The 144-page NCLT order sets out how the nature of Chandra's personal guarantees, the claims admitted in the proceedings and the creditors' voting ultimately shaped the decision.There were 23 creditors in the process, of which seven financial lenders voted against the resolution plan submitted by Chandra. Six creditors did not vote, while 10 creditors, comprising LPs, trustees, advisers and distributors, voted in favour of the plan. The plan secured the requisite majority, leading to its approval by the NCLT. Co.)0.06%Did not vote9Corpcall Capital Advisors LLP10.30%Favour10Direct Media Distribution Ventures Pvt. Ltd1.15%Favour11HDFC Bank Limited3.17%Against12IDBI Trusteeship (Edelweiss Fund)2.60%Did not vote13IDBI Trusteeship (Franklin Templeton)3.36%Against14Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited1.98%Favour15IndusInd Bank Limited1.11%Did not vote16Kautilya Traders Pvt Ltd1.02%Favour17Lemonade Capital Advisors LLP16.85%Favour18LIC Housing Finance6.09%Against19RBL Bank Limited0.55%Against20Sunil Jain0.18%Favour21Union Bank of India (UK) Ltd.0.76%Against22Veena Investments Private Limited4.99%Favour23World Crest Advisors28.49%Favour24Total100.00%Background: What is the case?Various entities of the Essel Group, promoted by Dr Subhash Chandra, had raised credit from 23 creditors. These creditors included banks, NBFCs, HFCs, asset reconstruction companies, investment entities and individuals, among others.Chandra had executed deeds standing as a personal guarantor for loans taken by these entities. He had not borrowed the money personally, but had provided personal guarantees for companies such as Vivek Infracon Pvt Ltd, which had borrowed from Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd, now Sammaan Capital Ltd.When the principal borrowers, including various Essel Group entities, failed to meet their repayment obligations, the creditors invoked Chandra’s personal guarantees under the IBC. The creditors subsequently filed claims aggregating Rs 22,006 crore in the proceedings. Sammaan Capital also approached the NCLT against Chandra.Chandra’s proposalChandra subsequently submitted a proposal to the creditors offering Rs 6.5 crore against claims of Rs 22,006 crore. Several creditors opposed the proposal because of the low recovery and the resulting 99.97% haircut. However, the plan received support from creditors representing about 80% of the voting share. Advt ‘Voting share’ here means the proportion of the total voting rights held by each creditor, based on the value of its admitted claim, rather than simply the number of creditors.Judiciary viewThe original two-member NCLT bench, comprising Judicial Member Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj and Member Reena Sinha Puri, differed in their views on the plan. The matter was subsequently referred to a third member.Member Puri had raised concerns over associate-party participation and the adequacy of due diligence on the claims. NCLT President subsequently referred the matter to Judicial Member Nilesh Sharma as the third member. Advt In the final order, Sharma approved the plan proposed by Chandra under Section 114 of the IBC. The tribunal held that it could not substitute its judicial assessment for the commercial wisdom of the majority of creditors who had approved the plan.The IBC requires approval by the prescribed majority of creditors by voting share. rows.title: Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are set to challenge the NCLT’s approval of Zee founder Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, which was cleared with 80.81 per cent of the creditors’ voting share despite opposition from several banks and public financial institutions. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Aug 31, 2026 at 12:55 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133636503; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Lenders including HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are moving against the NCLT’s approval of Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, with the lenders questioning the voting process and the eligibility of certain creditors who backed the proposal.Union Bank of India (UK) said it had rejected the plan along with lenders including Canara Bank and LIC Housing Finance and would "immediately" challenge the NCLT decision before the NCLAT. LIC Housing Finance said it would file an appeal along with other public financial institutions. HDFC Bank, which had a 3.17 per cent voting share, said it had opposed and voted against the resolution and was exploring an appeal. Advt The repayment plan, submitted by Chandra on October 16, 2024, was approved with 80.814 per cent of the voting share. The largest votes in favour came from World Crest Advisors (28.49 per cent), Lemonade Capital Advisors (16.85 per cent), Catalyst Trusteeship (11.85 per cent), Corpcall Capital Advisors (10.30 per cent) and Veena Investments (4.99 per cent).Among those voting against were LIC Housing Finance (6.09 per cent), IDBI Trusteeship representing Franklin Templeton (3.36 per cent), HDFC Bank (3.17 per cent), Axis Bank (2.86 per cent), Canara Bank (1.60 per cent), Union Bank of India (UK) (0.76 per cent) and RBL Bank (0.55 per cent). Creditors representing another 4.10 per cent did not vote.The dissenting lenders had argued that five entities - Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors and Corpcall Capital Advisors, were associates of Chandra and should therefore not have been allowed to vote. Together, the five represented about 61.78 per cent of the voting share.They also raised concerns over the speed of the process. Chandra submitted the plan on October 16, the Resolution Professional filed his report on October 17, and the creditors’ meeting was held on October 24. Creditors were asked to evaluate claims of around Rs 21,697 crore, with the voting period later extended to October 31. Advt The lenders had also questioned the adequacy of Chandra’s asset disclosures and sought an independent forensic audit and asset-tracing exercise. They pointed to earlier net-worth certificates showing his wealth at Rs 45,888 crore in 2017 and Rs 40,562 crore in 2018, compared with a current net worth of around Rs 31.79 crore cited in the proceedings.The NCLT itself saw a split in the matter. The Technical Member had found procedural violations, including the shortened timeline for the creditors’ meeting, and questioned the participation of alleged associates in the voting process.The Judicial Member, however, held that the creditors had sufficient practical opportunity to examine the plan, noting that the voting period had been extended and that the creditors ultimately approved the plan by the requisite majority. Advt The matter was subsequently referred to a Third Member because of the difference between the two members. The Third Member backed approval of the repayment plan, subject to certain directions including exclusion of specified claims from the final creditor list. rows.title: Bharat Ka Share Bazaar @ INDIA INTERNATIONAL TRADE FAIR – 2025
rows.desc: भारत का शेयर बाजार @ INDIA INTERNATIONAL TRADE FAIR – 2025 The ‘India International Trade Fair’ (IITF) is one of the largest trade fairs in the world, will be held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi from November 14 to 27, 2025. This year’s theme, ‘Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat’, highlights India’s cultural diversity and development. The IITF is a platform that has been used by various Regulators in the financial sector and other State and Government Institutions to spread awareness about their policies and programs among the public. In order to spread awareness, SEBI along with other securities market institutions has been setting up pavilion “भारत का शेयर बाजार” for last 10 years. Considering the huge success of previous years’ events, SEBI along with BSE, NSE, MCX, NCDEX, AMFI, CDSL, NSDL, NISM, CAMS and Kfintech has taken part in the 44 th IITF 2025, at Hall No-3, Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi. Join us at IITF 2025! Visit SEBI Pavilion “भारत का शेयर बाजार” –  Participate in our daily quiz, test your Knowledge and win exciting prizes.  Protect yourself from cyber investment fraud related to securities market through our initiatives like “SEBI Check”, Document Identification Verification System, etc.  Learn about securities market and get insights from the experts.  Experiential learning through “प्रततभूतत लेन देन तिमुलेशन (Securities transaction Simulation)”  On the spot KYC updation, nomination updation and other investor related services at our Investor Assistance Centre.  Update yourself about various cyber investment frauds related to securities market and their prevention through interactive activities i.e. “Nukkad Natak”, “Muppet shows” etc. Don’t miss this opportunity towards Investor education and awareness. Open to all! Block your Dates!

Submit your service requests with zero hassles with our seamless user experience Easy Access ONE to All ONE to All One service request is now enough to add, modify information across all your Mutual Fund folios Comprehensive All Mutual Funds All Mutual Funds MFCentral is a unified services gateway for all your mutual funds Safe Highly Secure Highly Secure MFCentral is a highly secure platform with multiple layers of protection & data encryption to perform your MF transactions Introducing India’s First All-in-one Investment Management Platform to Transform the Mutual Fund Industry MFCentral is the investor services hub conceived by KFintech & CAMS powering a new era of collaboration by providing convenience to transact across all folios of an investor with unparalleled user experience. Leveraging best in class technology, MFCentral brings ease, convenience and speed to your service requirements across all the Mutual Funds. View your Mutual Fund portfolio like a PRO! Now view your portfolio across all the Mutual Funds on a single platform! Slice and dice your assets based on asset class, fund house, returns, scheme level holdings and performance. View Now Managing your service requests can't get any SIMPLER! Out with paper, in with digital. Explore a range of services such as bank mandate change to updating your personal contact details to change in IDCW and more. Get the change done across all your folios with just a single request! Get Started Quick Links Easy access for seamless experience Update PAN Details Apply for PAN Transmission Request Transfer of units MITRA What’s New Positive Pay System (PPS) for cheques Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had announced introduction of Positive Pay System in Sept. 2020 to introduce an additional layer security for cheques above of Rs.50,000. Alternative Investment Fund and Foreign Portfolio Investors Department (AFD)

AFD handles all work related to Alternative Investment Funds (AIF), Venture Capital Funds (VCF), Foreign Venture Capital Investors (FVCI), Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPI), Designated Depository Participant (DDP) and Custodians.

Communications Department (CD)

The division would be responsible for all communications of SEBI. These include: 
- Media releases and other forms of communication including the publication of SEBI materials.
- News conferences and responding to inquiries from the press.
Corporation Finance Department (CFD)

The Corporation Finance Department deals with matters relating to
 (i)  Issuance and listing of securities, including initial and continuous listing requirements 
 (ii) Corporate governance and accounting/auditing standards 
 (iii) Corporate restructuring through Takeovers / buy backs
 (iv)  Social Stock Exchange- Policy Formulation, Regulatory Supervision, Creation of eco-system etc. 
 (v) Delisting etc.

 (Non Agriculture)
Department of Debt and Hybrid Securities (DDHS)

The Department of Debt and Hybrid Securities is responsibe for matters related to Corporate Bonds, listed debt securities, Real Estate Investment Trust, Infrastructure Investment Trust, deemed public issues of debt securities and complaints in respect of aforementioned areas of work.
Enforcement Department - 1 (EFD1)
Contents required from department.
Enquiries and Adjudication Department (EAD)

The Enquiries and Adjudication Department would handle quasi-judicial matters and provide timely hearings and initiates adjudication brought by the other Departments  against alleged violators who are within SEBI's disciplinary jurisdiction.
